summary.text: A 27-year-old nulliparous woman with a history of subfertility, low ovarian reserve and a multi-fibroid uterus, who had spontaneously conceived after 3 years of trying, presented at a routine dating scan at 13 + 1 weeks gestation with left-sided abdominal pain. On examination her abdomen was soft and diffusely tender in the suprapubic region.

The initial dating transabdominal ultrasound was reported as a probable intrauterine pregnancy, and the combined screening test gave increased chances for trisomies 21, 13 and 18 with a very low PAPP-A. Repeat transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound showed an extrauterine pregnancy with an empty uterine cavity; handheld ultrasound and same-day MRI showed a left adnexal pregnancy, which MRI presumed to be tubal. The implantation site could not be identified on ultrasound. Blood tests were obtained.

The patient was informed of the findings, surgical management was recommended, and a consultant-led multi-disciplinary team managed the case. Diagnostic laparoscopy found a live pregnancy enveloped by omentum with extensive adhesions; with ongoing active resuscitative measures and active haemorrhage the operation was converted to laparotomy, small and large bowel serosa had adherent trophoblastic tissue, trophoblast was excised, and a left salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Blood loss was 2000 mL with transfusion of red cells and plasma and one night in the ICU.

Histology confirmed a para-ovarian abdominal ectopic pregnancy with decidualised cells in the omentum, salpingitis with partially infarcted chorionic villi, and a left ovary with corpus luteum, congestion and surface granulation tissue.

She was discharged on day 9 post-operatively after recovery from post-operative ileus, completed outpatient follow-up with serum BhCG declining to below 15 IU/L after 3 weeks, and was re-referred to fertility services and for psychological support. She reported that the impact of losing a wanted pregnancy was greater than the physical sequelae.
